Lessons.Title: The Size of Angles on a Clock
ExplanationParagraphs: Source goal: describe the size of an angle as the turning of one ray to another. IM/Kendall Hunt 2021 Grade 4 Unit 7 Lesson 7 models this using clock hands and the centre as the shared vertex. The objective is reasoning about turns, not using longer drawn arms or blindly measuring a printed clock.

Warm-up (10 minutes) — Notice and Wonder: Two Sets of Angles. Use the legally available original source figures or independently authored versions; inspect each angle opening and communicate observations. No original pixel-accurate artwork is claimed.

Activity 1 (15 minutes) — Draw Angles Andre's Way. Andre says to imagine both clock hands at 12, then turn the minute hand to point to 3. One hand stays at 12; one turns clockwise a QUARTER of a full turn. Draw two rays sharing the clock centre, one to 12 and one to 3. Partner checks the construction and explanation.

Activity 2 (20 minutes) — Compare Angles on the Clock. The original Student Facing includes drawn clock-hand angle pairs such as 5:00. The teacher must inspect each original source pair and the child's diagrams. At exact hours, the minute hand points at 12, so the smaller opening to hour h spans min(h,12−h) hour-mark steps. This numerical formula is optional internal authoring; learners can reason by counting 1/12-turn spaces.

For exact-hour worked examples, 5:00 is five hour-mark steps (150°) and 6:00 is six (180°); at 8:00 the smaller angle is four steps (120°) between the 8 and 12 hands. These angles are first-party clock models and do not assert that publisher source image measurements were read.

First-party Edulytics Cool-down (5 minutes, not the protected original Which Angle Is Larger? By How Much?): compare the smaller openings at exactly 5:00 and exactly 8:00; explain which is larger and by how many hour-mark intervals. 5:00 is larger by one interval, or 30°, if degrees are known.

Digital Practice: eight first-party pairs of EXACT-hour clock faces. Question kind 0 selects A larger/B larger/equal, and kind 1 asks the nonnegative difference in one-hour-mark intervals. Do not apply this exact-hour simplification to half-past times or imply that student source clock drawings/partner work are automatically assessed.

KeyConcepts.Title: A clock's centre as vertex
KeyConcepts.Definition: The hands of an analog clock can represent two rays sharing the centre as their vertex.
KeyConcepts.Rule: At an exact hour, the minute hand is precisely at 12; the hour hand is precisely on that hour mark.
KeyConcepts.Example: Andre's 12-to-3 hand turn forms a quarter-turn angle.

KeyConcepts.Title: Count smaller clock turns
KeyConcepts.Definition: A full clock has 12 equal hour-mark gaps, each a twelfth of one full turn; the smaller opening at a whole hour covers at most 6 such gaps.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Between 12 and exact hour h, smaller gap count is min(h, 12−h); stop at six gaps for half a turn.
KeyConcepts.Example: At exactly 5:00, gap count is 5; at exactly 8:00, smaller gap count is 4.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compare by amount of turn
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two clock-hand angles can be compared by how many equal intervals separate their arms.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Count equal gaps and subtract gap counts to say how much larger. Ignore hand length.
KeyConcepts.Example: 5:00 is larger than 8:00 by one 1/12-turn interval.

WorkedExamples.Title: Andre's drawing from 12 to 3
WorkedExamples.Question: Both hands start pointing to 12. The minute hand turns clockwise until it points at 3. Draw the angle and describe the turn.
WorkedExamples.Method: Mark clock centre P, then draw rays from P toward 12 and 3.
Steps: Both rays start at the clock centre P.
The movement from 12 through 1, 2, to 3 spans three equal hour marks.
Three of twelve equal turns is a quarter of one full turn.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A quarter-turn angle at P, represented by rays pointing to 12 and 3.
WorkedExamples.Check: Original student sketch and oral explanation must be teacher-reviewed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Exact-hour 5:00 angle
WorkedExamples.Question: At exactly 5:00, what is the smaller angle between the hour and minute hands in hour-mark intervals?
WorkedExamples.Method: Minute hand at 12, hour hand at 5, and count the shorter path.
Steps: From 12 clockwise to 5 spans five hour gaps.
Counterclockwise spans seven, so the smaller is five.
The five hour gaps equal 5/12 full turn (150°).
WorkedExamples.Check: 150° is valid only for exactly 5:00; do not use for 5:30.

WorkedExamples.Title: Exact-hour 8:00 angle
WorkedExamples.Question: At exactly 8:00, what is the smaller angle between the hands?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare the two paths from 12 to 8; choose shorter.
Steps: Clockwise 12 to 8 spans eight hour marks.
The smaller opening is four gaps, equivalent to 120°.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare exact-hour 5:00 with 8:00
WorkedExamples.Question: Which smaller clock angle is larger at exactly 5:00 or exactly 8:00, and by how many intervals?
WorkedExamples.Method: Count the smaller opening on each complete clock face.
Steps: Exactly 5:00 gives five equal hour gaps.
Five exceeds four by one gap.
WorkedExamples.Check: Recognise the relative turn, not a long or short printed hand.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original source two sets and clock diagrams (teacher-scored)
WorkedExamples.Question: Inspect each original 2021 Two Sets of Angles/Compare Angles on the Clock picture and explain which displayed angle is larger.
WorkedExamples.Method: Trace the real rays/hands from the common vertex and compare the pictured turns.
Steps: Use authorised original diagrams or independent substitutes; do not assume images match text-only models.
Mark the two arms and which turning direction the diagram asks about.
Student draws or explains; teacher checks each original picture and reasoning.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Depends on actual original source figures, teacher-scored.
WorkedExamples.Check: No fabricated publisher picture-figure parity or exact clock image values are asserted.

WorkedExamples.Title: First-party Cool-down (teacher-scored explanation)
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare exactly 5:00 with exactly 8:00 and explain which smaller angle is larger and by how much in clock hour intervals.
WorkedExamples.Method: Count from 12 by the shorter path for both clocks.
Steps: Compare and give the difference in one equal interval.
WorkedExamples.Check: Not a reproduction of the inaccessible original publisher Cool-down.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating 8:00 as eight hour-mark steps for the smaller angle.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The shorter opening from 12 to 8 runs backward through four marks.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count both routes around the clock and use the shorter path.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Applying exact-hour formulas to half-hour drawings.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: At times like 5:30, the hour hand has moved away from the precise 5 position.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Only use the exact-hour shortcut when minutes are 00 and both hand positions are established.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming the original source clock-pair order or artwork was verified digitally.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The recorded original Student Facing excerpts do not provide all the needed actual diagrams.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Teacher checks original figures, hands, ray directions, drawings and explanations.

SummaryPoints: A clock centre is a common ray vertex; a hand turn changes the angular opening.
A 12-to-3 move is a quarter turn (three hour-mark intervals).
At exact hours, the smaller angle has at most six 1/12-turn gaps; 5:00=5, 8:00=4.
The first-party comparison family asks which is larger and by how many intervals, not original protected clock-figure interpretation.
Original source drawings, third-party pictures and gated Cool-down remain teacher-reviewed.
